questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Additional protection owed to a vulnerable group
questions.learningObjective: Name the elements of additional protection owed to a vulnerable group.
questions.stem: An analyst's dashboard note records a survey that enrolled 40 adults over 75 and 12 people learning English as a second language. Name the two elements of additional protection owed to the more vulnerable group.

options.text: Extra consent safeguards such as a supporter's presence and a plain-language consent process
A shorter consent form and a verbal summary of the study's purpose at the end
options.misconception: Treats reduced reading load as sufficient extra protection

options.text: Exclusion from the study, so that the group avoids any research burden
options.misconception: Assumes excluding participants is the appropriate protection

options.text: A larger sample of the group, so their answers carry more statistical weight
options.misconception: Confuses sample size with protection from risk

questions.explanation: Additional protection means extra safeguards around consent, such as a supporter present or plain-language materials. Removal from the study is not protection, and a larger sample adds no safeguard.
questions.hint: Safeguards around consent and participation.

options.misconception: Puts internal documentation ahead of protecting those affected

options.text: Assess and contain the breach, then determine whether individuals must be told without undue delay

options.text: Ask the contractor to sign a new confidentiality undertaking before any further action
options.misconception: Makes paperwork with the recipient a prerequisite for responding

questions.explanation: A breach triggers containment and assessment, then notification of affected individuals where warranted, without undue delay. A review or new paperwork may follow, but neither replaces telling those affected.

questions.topic: A retention schedule that enforces destruction
questions.learningObjective: Calculate how many records a retention schedule requires to be destroyed.
questions.stem: The dashboard note lists 1,240 order lines awaiting disposal under a retention schedule that frees a line once it is three years old. Three in every eight lines on the list are now old enough. How many lines must be destroyed?
questions.explanation: Three eighths of 1,240 is 465, because 1,240 divided by 8 is 155 and 155 times 3 is 465. Destroying the whole list, or only a part-eligible quarter, misapplies the three-year rule.

questions.topic: A de-identification claim in a published paper

questions.stem: The dashboard note shows that a paper claimed its released data were de-identified. Put the steps for checking that claim in the correct order.

options.text: Recount the unique combinations, then remove every row that appears more than once, then publish
options.misconception: Destroys the dataset instead of assessing the claim

options.text: Compare the paper's claim with the count of released rows, then recount the unique combinations afterwards
options.misconception: Starts the check without the reference count it needs

options.text: Recount the released rows unique on the quasi-identifiers, then compare that count with the paper's claim
Count the columns in the released file, then assume the claim holds because no names appear
options.misconception: Judges de-identification by column headings rather than rows

questions.explanation: The recount of unique combinations comes first, since the comparison with the published claim is the test. Counting columns decides nothing, and deleting rows destroys the evidence the check needs.
questions.hint: Recount first, compare second.

options.misconception: Confuses the claim with confirmation of a published conclusion

options.text: The whole pipeline, because archived code implies the data and environment were archived too
options.misconception: Assumes the code archive contains the inputs it consumes

options.text: Nothing at all, because a reproducibility claim without data is meaningless in every respect
options.misconception: Treats the code archive as worthless rather than partial

options.text: Only the transformation steps, since without data and environment details the code cannot be rerun end to end

questions.explanation: The claim covers only what the archive supports, here the transformation code, and cannot promise an end-to-end rerun without data and environment files. Assuming the archive holds its inputs misdescribes the deposit.
questions.hint: Check what the archive actually contains.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a data management plan must specify
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a data management plan must specify about handling data.
questions.stem: The dashboard note says a funding body asked for a data management plan. Explain what such a plan has to specify about the handling of the data it describes.

answer.exemplar: A data management plan has to describe what data will be collected, in what formats and volumes, how they will be stored and secured, who will be responsible for access, what naming and organisation conventions will be used, how documentation and metadata will be maintained, what retention and destruction periods will apply, and what will happen if the project ends, including any costs and the arrangements for preservation or archiving of the material.

questions.explanation: The plan must cover the data's whole life, from collection through storage, access, documentation, preservation and disposal. Listing only formats and storage locations leaves the harder commitments out.
questions.hint: Follow the data through its whole life.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why full anonymisation is often impossible
questions.learningObjective: Explain why full anonymisation is often impossible for distinctive data.

stimulus.body: The dashboard describes a dataset of unique customer transactions with a stable account identifier, and the owner asks for it to be published with no link back to any person.

questions.stem: Given the contents of that dataset, why is full anonymisation usually impossible here?

options.text: Because the account identifier column is present and must be deleted for the data to count as anonymous
options.misconception: Believes removing one identifier column is enough for full anonymity

options.text: Because the transactions are few and distinctive, so each row remains identifiable from its own content
Because the customers paid by card, so any published row can be traced through the payment scheme
options.misconception: Assumes payment method alone prevents anonymisation

options.text: Because the dataset is small, and any small dataset should simply be withheld rather than published
options.misconception: Equates smallness with a duty not to publish at all

questions.explanation: When rows are few and distinctive, their content can single a person out even without an identifier column, so meaningful anonymisation cannot be guaranteed. Deleting the account column is not enough, and size is no reason to withhold.
questions.hint: Look at what each row reveals on its own.

options.misconception: Confuses financial cover with the protective process itself

options.text: An opt-out process, so that children can leave the study without explaining why
options.misconception: Treats opt-out as the distinctive feature of extra protection

A smaller sample of children, which lowers the risk that the study poses to any child

options.text: Confirm that no column is named contact, then report the paper's de-identification claim as verified
options.misconception: Treats a column name as the whole of the de-identification question

Check whether the paper mentions a key, then report that the data are anonymous if it does

options.misconception: Relies on the authors' opinion instead of testing the release

options.misconception: Assumes the image is portable in a way the note never claims

options.text: Whether the archived image pins the software versions used for the published analysis
options.misconception: Treats version pinning as something the image cannot do

options.text: Whether the underlying data were retained and are available to anyone checking the claim
Whether the scripts inside the image reproduce the figures printed in the paper
options.misconception: Denies the very reproducibility the image is offered to support

questions.explanation: An archived container pins the environment and code but says nothing about whether the data behind the results exist and are reachable. Version pinning and portability are what an image is for.

questions.topic: Why full anonymisation is often impossible
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the steps for judging whether full anonymisation is achievable.
questions.stem: The dashboard note plans to release a dataset of household transactions. Put the steps for judging whether full anonymisation is achievable in the correct order.

options.text: Ask the data owner to confirm the dataset is anonymous, then record the confirmation as the finding
options.misconception: Relies on an assurance instead of a linkage test

options.text: Judge whether rows are indistinguishable, then test linkage only if the dataset looks risky
options.misconception: Draws the conclusion before gathering the evidence

options.text: Remove the obvious identifiers, then publish the dataset because no name fields remain
options.misconception: Stops at the weakest step and treats it as complete

options.text: Test linkage against plausible outside sources, then judge whether the remaining rows stay indistinguishable

questions.explanation: The judgement rests on evidence about linkage, so plausible outside sources must be tested before a conclusion is drawn. Removing obvious identifiers is a first step, and an owner's assurance is not a linkage test.

options.misconception: Treats a proxy signature as a substitute for the participant's own view

options.text: Proxy consent requires extra safeguards, since the participant's own view cannot be obtained directly
The trial needs no additional protection, because both groups are adults with capacity
options.misconception: Assumes adult status alone settles the protection question

options.misconception: Points the protection at the wrong member of the pair

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Duties after a data breach
questions.learningObjective: Explain the duties that follow a data breach.
questions.stem: A dashboard note records that a laptop holding a customer export was stolen from a parked car. Explain what the responding organisation has to do after the breach.

answer.exemplar: The organisation must contain the breach by securing the device and accounts, assess what was taken and the likely harm, and then decide whether to notify the affected individuals and the relevant regulator, without undue delay and on the facts it has. It also has to log the incident, follow up whether the data can be recovered, and review the controls that let it happen, while keeping its documentation of the assessment for any later scrutiny by the regulator or the affected customers.

questions.explanation: The response covers containing the breach, assessing risk to people, and notifying where warranted without undue delay, with a record of the decision. Treating containment or an apology as the whole duty is the error.
questions.hint: Contain, assess, notify, record.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a reproducibility claim does not cover
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a partial reproducibility claim leaves unaddressed.
questions.stem: The dashboard carries a reproducibility statement covering the analysis code and one intermediate table. Explain what such a claim leaves unaddressed.

answer.exemplar: A claim that covers the code and one intermediate table leaves the earlier stages of the work unsupported: the raw inputs may not be in the archive, the steps that produced the intermediate table may not be documented, and anyone checking the claim would have to rebuild those stages themselves. It also leaves open whether the archived artefacts correspond to the published version, which is exactly the part a reader needs in order to judge the claim for themselves rather than take it on trust.

questions.explanation: A partial claim is honest about its scope but says nothing about the stages it omits, and readers cannot judge results they cannot rebuild. Treating archived artefacts as proof the whole chain was preserved is the error.
questions.hint: Ask what a checker would still have to rebuild.

answer.exemplar: The claim has to be tied to a specific released file, a stated set of quasi-identifiers, and a described test, so that a reader can say what was attempted and what it failed to rule out. questions.topic: Additional protection owed to a vulnerable group
questions.learningObjective: Interpret what extra consent steps represent for a vulnerable group.

stimulus.body: The dashboard records a study of hospital patients who are asked to review a service change, and the protocol gives those patients a longer consent conversation and a scheduled follow-up call.

questions.stem: Given that protocol, what do the extra steps represent?

options.text: Evidence of low risk, since extra steps would only be needed where the study was risky
options.misconception: Treats the safeguards as a signal about the risk level instead of protection

options.text: Good manners, since the extra steps make the sessions more pleasant for participants
options.misconception: Reduces a protective requirement to a courtesy

options.text: A pilot exercise, because the extra steps are provisional until the main study starts
options.misconception: Reads the safeguards as a temporary trial arrangement

options.text: Additional protection, because the safeguards were added for the specific vulnerability of the group

questions.explanation: Extra consent steps and a follow-up call are additional protection where the ordinary process is less than sufficient, and the note should record which vulnerability prompted them. Courtesy, provisional status and a risk signal misread their purpose.
questions.hint: Extra steps for extra vulnerability.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Duties after a data breach
questions.learningObjective: State the duties that follow a breach most accurately.
questions.stem: The dashboard note sets out the duties that follow a breach. Which one is stated most accurately?

options.text: Tell everyone affected within 24 hours, whatever the risk turns out to be
options.misconception: Fixes a universal deadline that the standard does not impose

options.text: Containment, a risk assessment for people and notification without undue delay, with urgency set by the risk
Notify only when the breach has caused measurable financial loss to the organisation
options.misconception: Makes notification depend on the organisation's own loss

options.text: Publish a full public account of the breach before taking any containment step
options.misconception: Ranks transparency above containment of the exposure

questions.explanation: Containment, a risk assessment for people and notification without undue delay, with urgency set by the risk. Organisational loss is not the trigger, and publishing early exposes information.
questions.hint: Urgency follows the risk, not a fixed clock.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A retention schedule that enforces destruction
questions.learningObjective: Calculate how many records a retention schedule requires to be destroyed.
questions.stem: The dashboard note lists 900 records due for disposal under a retention schedule, and 60 per cent of them meet the condition for immediate destruction. How many records must be destroyed?
questions.explanation: Sixty per cent of 900 is 540, because 900 divided by 100 is 9 and 9 times 60 is 540. Destroying the whole list, or applying the percentage to survivors, misapplies the schedule's condition.
questions.hint: Find one per cent, then multiply.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A de-identification claim in a published paper
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the steps for reviewing a de-identification claim before publication.
questions.stem: The dashboard note plans how a de-identification claim will be reviewed before publication. Put the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Check the released rows for uniqueness, then publish the file before any linkage test is attempted
options.misconception: Releases the data before the risk has been assessed

options.text: Test linkage against outside sources, then check the released rows for uniqueness and publish without comment
options.misconception: Omits the step that reports what the test covered

options.text: Check the released rows for uniqueness, test linkage against outside sources, then state the limits tested
State the limits of the test first, then check uniqueness and linkage to see whether the statement holds
options.misconception: Writes the conclusion before doing the work

questions.explanation: The review must establish the facts about the rows, test them against outside sources and report what was covered. Releasing before the test or writing the conclusion first inverts the assessment.
questions.hint: Facts, test, then reported limits.
